4 Discussion

Here, we applied a computational model of momentary happiness which assumes fluctuations in affect ratings depend simply on baseline affect, its drift over time, and recency-decayed expected and received outcomes. By extending this model to also capture learning, we were able to link objective behaviour to subjective feelings across distinct affective states-happiness, confidence, and engagement ratings-and show that a core component of psychological therapy, cognitive distancing, and antidepressant medication use have different effects on affective dynamics, but converge to alter affective biases associated with symptoms of mental ill-health.

There were distinct effects of both treatments on affective dynamics. Randomisation to a psychotherapeutic intervention, cognitive distancing, attenuated declines in happiness and, more tentatively, engagement over the course of the task, adding to our previously reported findings that this psychotherapeutic technique alters aspects of reward learning 41 . Self-reported antidepressant use, meanwhile, was associated with higher baseline happiness and confidence after adjustment for current anxiety/depression symptoms (as antidepressant use was not randomised), which is consistent with evidence that antidepressants exert positive affective biases 64 . Subsequent exploration of changes in affect revealed further mechanistic divergence: current antidepressant use was associated with lower recency biases for happiness and engagement (i.e., forgetting factors closer to one), and cognitive distancing reduced the weighting of expectations and increased recency bias in happiness ratings. Together, these results suggest that psychiatric treatments act to alter the contribution of objective learning-related quantities to subjective value judgements.

Consistent with extensive evidence 22, 26, 27, 65 , we found negative associations between model-derived baseline affect (across all scales) and transdiagnostic psychiatric symptom measures derived from computational factor modelling 45, 46 . This effect, which was strongest for anxiety/depression symptom scores, indicates a consistent, time-invariant negative affective bias which scales with mental ill-health symptom load. Critically, we found evidence for a convergent treatment by symptom interaction with baseline affect across both cognitive distancing and antidepressant use: negative associations between anxiety/depression symptoms and baseline happiness and confidence were attenuated in participants receiving either treatment. These results support the cognitive neuropsychological model of antidepressant action, whereby antidepressants are proposed to act acutely to reverse negative or maladaptive affective biases 21, 66 , and suggest that cognitive distancing 43 and other components of psychotherapy may also act clinically to alter affective biases contributing to symptoms of mental ill-health. We propose that changes in affective dynamics should be investigated further in longitudinal studies as a computational predictor of subsequent symptom change.

Our methodological approach also extends previous work in two ways. First, we applied a theory-driven computational model which allows for fluctuations in momentary happiness as a function of the history of expected values and prediction errors resulting from those expectations, which has been primarily validated in tasks where learning is not required 5 . We show not only that this model can capture happiness ratings in a task where expected values are never explicitly available and have to be learned from experience, but also that it can accurately capture variation in subjective ratings of confidence and engagement. Second, we found evidence for drift in happiness over time, replicating recent work which characterised "mood drift over time" 54 and extending this to both confidence and engagement.

Affective drift has been proposed to reflect the increasing opportunity cost of remaining engaged, with mood serving as an adaptive signal of the value of continuing (exploiting) rather than switching away from the task (exploring) 54 . This offers a candidate mechanism for our finding that distancing attenuated drift in happiness: both here and in previous work 41 , distancing participants showed higher inverse temperatures (Figure S2B-C in the Supplementary Methods), indicating more exploitative choice. Although the inverse temperature cannot distinguish random exploration from other sources of choice variability, in this account attenuated drift and less stochastic choice may both reflect a common shift away from exploration. We emphasise that this account remains speculative, and that our findings diverged from previous work in two respects: first, rather than reduced drift with increased depressive symptoms during risky decision-making 54 , we found moderate-tostrong evidence to the contrary during RL (Figure 2Aii); and second, drift was strongly associated with self-reported fatigue (Figure S5; see Supplementary Results), which has been proposed to be mechanistically distinct from the boredom that may partly underlie mood drift 15 . Both divergences may reflect the demands of our task: where mood drift was previously characterised in rest periods and tasks in which reward contingencies did not have to be learned 54 , sustained learning may render affective drift sensitive to fatigue, meaning that associations between affective drift and symptoms of mental ill-health are not task invariant and likely depend on task demands.

We note some important limitations in our measures. Transdiagnostic measures of mental health psychopathology were estimated using questionnaire subsets 41, 48 , precluding investigation of associations between parameters and individual diagnostic scales. Antidepressant use was self-reported and non-randomised, and we did not collect information concerning length of treatment, dosage, concurrent psychological therapies, or reason for prescription; we also could not compare across antidepressant classes, as the vast majority of those on antidepressants (70.8%) reported taking an SSRI (Table S3), though we note this is the class in which affective biases have been most extensively characterised 21.

We were likewise limited in how well we could characterise the distancing intervention: to minimise differences between groups in task procedure, we did not ask participants about how much they engaged with the intervention, and so lack a direct measure of adherence. We note, however, that self-rated enjoyment and concentration at the end of the task did not differ between groups, and while in-task baseline engagement (i.e., w engaged 0 ) was lower in the distancing group, this is arguably what one would expect of a technique premised on "taking a step back" from feedback; that this occurred without any corresponding reduction in self-reported concentration suggests emotional rather than attentional disengagement.

Further, cognitive distancing, especially as delivered here, should be considered a treatment component rather than a complete intervention: our parallel analyses with antidepressant use aim to identify points of mechanistic convergence and divergence as opposed to directly comparing the treatments.

We also note two methodological limitations. First, our use of a single computational model for all three affect scales is a powerful approach, but limited in its ability to truly contrast trial-to-trial fluctuations in each individual rating scale, as we are only comparing the contribution of a small number of computational components (i.e., affective weights) to a fraction of their variation; the residual (scale-specific) variation is likely also important in explaining how these ratings overlap and differ. This is particularly relevant where the constructs themselves remain contested: momentary confidence may reflect more than the probability a choice is correct 11, 12 , and momentary engagement may index the cost of effort itself or the accumulating cost of continuing 14, 15 . Our approach is deliberately agnostic between accounts, asking what can be read out from the trial-wise quantities known to drive choice rather than explaining what each rating specifically measures. The affect model could in principle be extended with additional weights to distinguish between these accounts, though this would only be informative in a task designed to dissociate quantities such as decision evidence 431 or effort costs from expected values and prediction errors, which ours was not. Second, as model 432 complexity meant only approximate (mean-field variational, rather than sampling-based) inference 433 was viable, we were unable to account for uncertainty in estimates of individual-level posterior 434 mean parameters in associations with quantities of interest (e.g., by using precision-weighted GLMs), 435 as the posterior covariance matrix cannot accurately capture local interdependencies, meaning that 436 parameter precisions are not reliable enough for uncertainty-weighted outcome models 55,67 . 437 To conclude, we integrated objective choice behaviour in a learning task with trial-to-trial affect 438 ratings across three distinct states-happiness, confidence, and engagement-within a unified com-439 putational model. This enabled us to uncover associations between model parameters and treatments 440 for mental health conditions, offering new insights into their underlying mechanisms of action. Our 441 results demonstrate the critical importance of affective biases in the maintenance and updating of 442 affective states in mental ill-health, and indicate that existing, effective treatments can be understood 443 at least in part as acting to shift these biases towards the healthy range. 444 Acronyms ADVI Automatic Differentiation Variational Inference BCa Bias-Corrected and accelerated CI Confidence Interval ELPD Expected Log Pointwise Predictive Density GLM Generalised Linear Model HDI Highest Density Interval HBREC Human Biology Research Ethics Committee LOO Leave One Out MCMC Markov Chain Monte Carlo MSE Mean Squared Error NHS National Health Service PLS Partial Least Squares RL Reinforcement Learning SD Standard Deviation SSRI Selective Serotonin Reuptake Inhibitor

Between-rating RL-affect model

Model definition and fit

In an exploratory analysis, we modified Equation 5 to partition the weights on expected values and prediction errors (w p 2 and w p 3 ) into individual weights on the outcomes of each trial since the last rating of that type (in our task, this could be up to four intervening outcomes plus the current trial).

As such, the lagged trial weight parameters w p 2 (-t ′ ) and w p 3 (-t ′ ) can be seen as capturing the betweenrating change in affective dynamics. We hence modify Equation 5 as follows, where I denotes the number of ratings between the current rating and the last rating of the same type; in this task, I ≤ 4. w p k (-t ′ ) are the weights on the outcomes t ′ trials back, so w p k (0) is the weight on the outcome of the current trial, w p k (-1) is the weight on the outcome of the previous trial, and so on.

To account for potential differences in how positive and negative surprises influence affect ratings, for example due to perceptual processing differences, we additionally considered an extended "signed" variant of this model. This model partitions the weight on prediction errors depending on their sign, allowing for different weights on positive and negative prediction errors. Denoting these weights as w p(+) 3 (-t ′ ) and w p(-)

Both models were fitted to choices and ratings on all three affect scales simultaneously in a hierarchical Bayesian manner via ADVI 55 as explained in Methods. The only difference was that lagged trial weights were assumed drawn from w p 2 and w p 3 priors specific to each individual which in turn were drawn from overall group-level hyperpriors (i.e., a three-level hierarchy). The fits of the unsigned and signed between-rating models were compared using ELPD-LOO as before.

Between-rating RL-affect model

Parameter recovery for the (unsigned) between-rating RL-affect model was tested similarly, with one hundred simulated datasets. The parameter settings were identical to the above except for the time-dependent parameters (and the absence of γ p in the model). Specifically, w p 2 (-t ′ ) and w p 3 (-t ′ ) were sampled from Beta(1, t ′ + 1) distributions, where t ′ is the trial lag, so that weights for earlier trials were weighted (on average) lower, as we see in the real dataset. Again, even with the high complexity of the model, we found that all parameters could be recovered with extremely high accuracy (r ≥ 0.95; Figure S1B).

Comparison between results from an RL model fitted to choices alone (with samplingbased inference) vs. the joint RL-affect model (with variational inference)

We previously reported results in this dataset where we fitted a dual learning rate Q-learning model to choices alone and compared parameters in distanced and non-distanced participants 41 . As the RL component of the winning joint RL-affect model in the present study was identical to this previously fitted model, we compared the estimated individual-level learning parameters between the two models. Antidepressant use is associated with increased weighting of previous choices' expected values in affect ratings

To further unpick the effects of treatments on the weighting of previous outcomes, we fitted more flexible between-rating RL-affect models (Equation 7and Equation 8). These models, which allowed for different weights on previous expected values and prediction errors since the previous rating (i.e., the current trial and up to four preceding trials), were able to capture the ratings well, albeit with marginally worse accuracy than the primary drift-over-time model presented in the main text (e.g., mean [SD] pseudo-R² for the unsigned between-rating RL-affect model = 0.38-0.39 [0.22-0.25] across all three ratings). There was no evidence that partitioning weights on prediction errors into separate positive and negative weights in an extended "signed" model improved the model fit (its estimated out-of-sample predictive accuracy was worse: ELPD-LOO difference [standard error] versus unsigned model = -1375.0 [494.0]), but for completeness we present results from both the unsigned and signed models (Figure S4).

We related w p 2 (-t ′ ) and w p(+) or (-) 3 (-t ′ ) for each rating type separately to both treatments via multilevel GLMs with participant-level random intercepts and slopes (on trial lag), adjusting for age, gender, and digit span as before.

Parameters from the between-rating models generally suggested no evidence for any difference between distancing and non-distancing participants in the weighting of the most recent or intervening outcomes in their affective judgements (Figure S4A). The only exception was weak-to-moderate evidence for lower weighting of positive prediction errors in happiness and confidence judgements in distancing individuals (multipliers [95% HDIs] = 0.982 [0.947, 1.01] and 0.972 [0.938, 1.004], P direction = 0.886 and 0.952 respectively; Figure S4Aii), with weak evidence for accompanying positive interaction effects, suggesting overall more weighting of intervening positive prediction errors in affect ratings (Figure S4Av).

There was no evidence of an effect of current antidepressant use on weightings of prediction errors from previous trials (Figure S4Bii-vi). There was, however, strong evidence of slightly higher weighting of the most recent expected value in subjective confidence and engagement ratings in those currently taking antidepressants (multipliers [95% HDIs] = 1.04 [1.01, 1.07] and 1.06 [1.01, 1.16], P direction = 0.995 and 0.993 respectively; Figure S4Bi), alongside evidence of negative interaction effects (Figure S4Biv), which together indicate a selective increase in the weighting of the most recent Though there was no evidence for any difference in the association between reward or loss learning rates and fatigue between distancing and non-distancing participants, there was evidence for a difference in association with inverse temperature, β (Figure S6Aiii & Figure S6Biii). Specifically, there was strong evidence for a negative distancing by fatigue interaction for both measures of fatigue, such that while there was no association between β and post-block fatigue (mean or change over time) in non-distanced participants, distanced participants had lower inverse temperatures (i.e., choices less determined by expected values) with increases in self-reported fatigue (e.g., mean [95% HDI] difference in change in β for a 10-point increase in mean post-block fatigue in distanced versus non-distanced participants = -0.129 [-0.278, -0.028], P direction = 0.990; Figure S6Aiii).

Taken with the results above (Figure S5), this suggests that while distancing participants' affect ratings reflected their fatigue less than non-distancing participants, their choices were more affected by fatigue than non-distancing participants, potentially due to the higher cognitive load they experienced during the task.

Interpretation of GLM-estimated weight effects

In the Results, effects of covariates on baseline affect (w p 0 ) have a relatively simple interpretation because the second-level GLMs for w p 0 are fitted to the participant-level intercepts after an inverse logit transformation: their coefficients (multiplied by 100) are simply differences in rating points between individuals differing only in the covariate of interest. Effects on the drift-over-time, expected value and prediction error weights (w p 1 , w p 2 , w p 3 ), meanwhile, are estimated on the log-odds scale, since these GLMs are fitted to the untransformed Beta regression weights. This means that, for example, a GLM coefficient for the distancing group of 0.1 in relation to w happy 1 for the primary time elapsed model (Equation 5) indicates that the hourly multiplicative change in the odds of mean happiness is exp(0.1) = 1.105 times greater in distanced than non-distanced participants. Similarly, multiplicative differences in w p 2 or w p 3 indicate a difference between groups in the multiplicative change in the odds of mean affect for a unit change in (decayed) expected values or prediction errors.

Clearly, these effects do not have obvious interpretations and cannot be directly transformed to the rating point scale, as a fixed difference in log-odds corresponds to a varying difference on the point scale depending on where on the scale it is applied. To aid in this, we calculate an estimated difference between reference individuals differing only in the covariate of interest (e.g., distanced versus non-distanced; one SD higher symptom score), with the same (mean for that rating type) baseline affect, and all other covariates held at their sample median or reference category. As this referenceindividual estimate is intended as an interpretive aid rather than a formal posterior summary, we report it as a point estimate alongside the multiplier, its 95% HDI, and P direction.

Alternative choice model parameterisations

Our primary model comparison considered two choice model parameterisations: Q-learning models with either one or two learning rates. This was primarily to maintain consistency with previous work, including the original models of choice behaviour in this task 40 , and our previous work in this sample 41.

However, differences in choice behaviour, and hence the extent to which choice-related quantities P R E P R I N T are reflected in affect ratings, might be better explained by alternative parameterisations. In particular, differences in choice behaviours related to anhedonia and depression may be better explained by (in)sensitivity to rewards (outcome sensitivity) than (in)sensitivity to prediction errors (learning rates) 59 . To test this proposal, we fitted a variant of our winning RL-affect model with a single learning rate and different sensitivities to rewards ("Correct!") and losses ("Incorrect."). This modifies Equation 1: where ρ reward and ρ loss are sensitivities to rewards and losses respectively; as these scale expected values directly, no separate inverse temperature β was estimated for this model.

Another explanation for choice biases stemming from alternative responses to feedback was proposed by Collins et al. [60]. Specifically, they introduce a "perseveration" parameter ζ which allows for potential neglect of negative feedback by reducing the rate of learning from negative prediction errors (α loss ) relative to the rate of learning from positive prediction errors (α reward ): We fitted joint RL-affect models incorporating both alternative choice model parameterisations in an identical manner to our primary model comparison, and then compared their fit to our primary (winning) model with dual learning rates. Based on the ELPD-LOO, we found no evidence to suggest that either of these alternative models had better estimated out-of-sample predictive accuracy than our winning model (Table S1).

Associations between between-rating RL-affect model parameters and treatments

The associations between the weights on expected values and prediction errors for individual trials and cognitive distancing and antidepressant use were quantified using multilevel Bayesian linear regression models implemented in the brms R package 68 , fitted with MCMC via the cmdstanr interface to CmdStan (v2.39.0) 56, 69 , with 2,000 warm-up and 4,000 sampling iterations for each of four chains. All models controlled for the same covariates (i.e., age, gender, digit span), but also included a participant-level random intercept and slopes (on trial lag) to account for the fact there were five parameters per person for each affect rating, as well as the main effect of trial lag and its interaction with each treatment. Separate models were fitted for each affect rating and parameter-ofinterest (e.g., w 2 (-t ′ ) and w 3 (-t ′ ) for the unsigned model).

Joint RL-affect model with affect drift over time

To test whether we could recover known parameter values from the best-fitting model (i.e., dual learning rate, time elapsed in hours), we simulated one hundred datasets (including choices and affect ratings) with parameters drawn from the distributions in Table S2.

Parameter estimates for the best-fitting joint RL-affect model

Across individuals, model-predicted baseline affect (w p 0 ) was highest for engagement (mean = 63.4 points; SD = 19.3), followed by happiness (mean = 55.8, SD = 17.3), and lowest for confidence (mean = 40.7, SD = 20.

1). Meanwhile, affect drift over time (w p 1 ) was steepest for engagement: individual-level median 45.2% lower odds of increased engagement per hour (all other terms being equal), compared to 38.3% lower confidence and 30.0% lower happiness per hour. Group-level means for weights on recent expected values (w p 2 ) and prediction errors (w p 3 ) were positive for all three ratings, showing higher affect with increased recent rewards, and were lowest for engagement (posterior mean [95% HDI] for multiplier: w happy2 = 1.177 [1.175, 1.179], w confident2 = 1.227 [1.225, 1.230], w engaged2 = 1.129 [1.128, 1.131]; w happy3 = 1.175 [1.174, 1.176], w confident3 = 1.219 [1.218, 1.221], w engaged3 = 1.119 [1.118, 1.120]). Lastly, the group-level mean decay factor was highest for confidence (mean = 0.543; 95% HDI = [0.541, 0.544]), and lowest for happiness (mean = 0.385; 95% HDI = [0.384, 0.386]), suggesting higher weighting of outcomes of earlier trials (i.e., prior to the most recent trial) in confidence judgements compared to happiness ratings.

Compulsive behaviour and social withdrawal factor scores are also associated with altered affective dynamics

In addition to differences in baseline affect and its drift over time, there was evidence that participants with higher transdiagnostic measures of mental ill-health differed in shorter-term affective dynamics.

Specifically, individuals with higher anxiety/depression factor scores placed more weight on recent prediction errors (higher w p 3 ), with strong evidence for higher w confident 3 (multiplier [95% HDI] = 1.01 [1.001, 1.023] for an SD increase in anxiety/depression score, P direction = 0.986). There was also strong evidence that those with higher compulsive behaviour scores placed more weight on recent prediction errors, and, to a lesser extent, recent expected values (higher w p 2 ; moderate evidence for higher w happy 2 only) in all of their subjective affect judgements (Figure S3Bii-iii).

The consequences of this were evident in the observed data. For example, there was strong statistical evidence for a small positive correlation between happiness rating variability and compulsive behaviour factor scores (correlation coefficient [95% CI] r = 0.150 [0.086, 0.212], p < 0.0001;

Figure S3D), which can also be qualitatively observed by comparing mean-centred happiness ratings for participants in the bottom quartile versus the top quartile of compulsive behaviour factor scores (Figure S3E). That said, the actual effect of the estimated differences in w happy 2 and w happy 3 on ratings is small, as shown by simulating happiness ratings for individuals who differ only in having the estimated w happy 2 and w happy 3 for those with the 25 th percentile versus the 75 th percentile compulsive behaviour factor score (Figure S3F).

We additionally found moderate evidence that increases in anxiety/depression factor were associated with slightly higher weighting of previous trials' expected values and prediction errors for happiness (γ happy ; e.g., previous trial weighted an estimated 2.77% higher; 95% HDI for multiplier = [0.999, 1.059], P direction = 0.967; Figure S3Aiii). There was also evidence for a positive association between social withdrawal factor score and decay factors for happiness and engagement (Figure S3Ciii), suggesting marginally higher weighting of previous trials' expected values and prediction errors in the computation of affect ratings in those with higher levels of social withdrawal symptoms.

Affect drift over time is associated with self-reported fatigue

Previous work on 'mood drift over time' has suggested it is mostly distinct from boredom and mind wandering 54 . Here, we were able to test an additional aspect of this phenomenon, namely its relation to fatigue, as we asked participants the following question after the end of each of the six blocks: "How fatigued do you feel compared to the beginning of the block?".

We hence examined the association between w p 1 and both participants' overall mean post-block fatigue and their change in post-block fatigue ratings over the course of the six training blocks. To quantify change in post-block fatigue, the six ratings were regressed on block number for each participant, with the regression coefficient (β ∆fatigue ) on block number taken as the quantity of interest (i.e., higher values suggest increases in post-block fatigue ratings over time). We found strong evidence, after adjusting for age, gender, digit span, and distancing group, that higher mean post-block fatigue ratings were associated with lower baseline affect (lower w p 0 ; Figure S5Ai) and decreased odds of higher affect ratings across the task (lower w p 1 ; Figure S5Aii), across all three affect rating types (e.g.,

Cognitive distancing does not act on fatigue to alter affective drift

In our primary analysis, we found that cognitive distancing specifically acted to slow drift in happiness and, to a lesser extent, engagement (Figure 3Aii). Given the strong associations between affect

To test this, we added an interaction term to the models described above, to test the between-group difference in associations between baseline affect and affective drift, and mean and change in post-block fatigue ratings.

We found strong evidence for an interaction between distancing and fatigue ratings in the as- Figure S5Aiii & Figure S5Biii), such that there were weaker associations between baseline happiness and confidence and fatigue ratings in distancing participants. In other words, fatigue was less reflected in baseline affect ratings in the distanced group, compared to non-distanced participants.

Crucially, however, we found no evidence of a difference in association between drift in happiness or engagement and either fatigue measure between groups, with weak evidence for differences in the effect of fatigue on confidence (Figure S5Aiv & Figure S5Biv). This suggests that the effect of distancing on affective drift is not explained by self-reported post-block fatigue.

Cognitive distancing alters associations between fatigue and inverse temperature

We additionally considered whether cognitive distancing may alter associations between Q-learning model parameters and post-block fatigue self-reports.

In distancing participants, each SD increase in anxiety/depression score was associated with 2.10-point higher baseline happiness (95% HDI = [-0.027, 4.21], P direction = 0.974) and 2.04point higher baseline confidence (95% HDI = [-0.409, 4.61], P direction = 0.943) than non-distancing participants (Figure 3Ci). A similar pattern was seen in those taking antidepressants, though the evidence was clearest for confidence: relative to participants not taking antidepressants with the same symptom levels, each SD increase in anxiety/depression score was associated with 5.07-point higher baseline confidence with strong evidence (95% HDI = [0.809, 9.26], P direction = 0.991), and, with (very) weak evidence, 1.44-point higher baseline happiness (95% HDI = [-2.10, 4.95], P direction = 0.785; Figure 3Cii).

In addition, regression coefficients capturing change in post-block fatigue were strongly negatively associated with w p 1 across all rating types after adjusting for mean post-block fatigue, most strongly for engagement (estimated 1.01-point lower engagement rating after an hour per one-pointper-block increased fatigue rating change; multiplier [95% HDI] = 0.907 [0.881, 0.933], P direction > 0.999; Figure S5Bii). Notably, associations in the opposite (positive) direction were observed between β ∆fatigue and baseline affect (w p 0 ), again most strongly for engagement (estimated 0.575-point increase in engagement rating per one-point-per-block increased fatigue rating for a reference individual; 95% HDI = [0.317, 0.846], P direction > 0.999; Figure S5Bi). Speculatively, this may represent an effect of motivation, where participants who were more engaged towards the beginning of the task also exerted more effort, resulting in larger overall increases in fatigue and decreases in engagement.
